summary: Proposes an experimental set of alternative decision-making processes for IETF working groups. It targets the rare cases where a group agrees a decision must be made but cannot agree on what the decision should be. The processes are experiments, and the document does not claim to be exhaustive.

eli5.summary: When a class all agree they must pick a game but cannot agree which, this memo offers some new ways to break the tie.

questions: how does the ietf break a deadlock
what happens when an ietf working group cannot agree
what is instant runoff voting in the ietf
how does an ietf external review team work
subtitle: Four experimental ways for an IETF working group to break a deadlock when it agrees a choice must be made but not which one.

tldr.problem: Sometimes an IETF working group agrees that it must pick one technical proposal, yet the competing proposals are about equally mature and the group cannot reach rough consensus on which one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets conditions for invoking an alternative and defines four methods: an external review team, a mixed review team, a qualified short-straw selection, and random assignment by IANA.
tldr.outcome: The methods are an experiment, not a replacement for rough consensus. The RFC says that if the community finds them useful, they should be documented in a BCP. It is updated by RFC 8717.

today: RFC 3929 is an Experimental RFC and is updated by RFC 8717. The text itself says the methods should be documented in a BCP only if the community becomes satisfied that they are useful.

sections.title: The Deadlock Problem
sections.content:
The IETF decides things by "rough consensus and running code". In a small number of cases a working group concludes that a decision must be made so that an interoperable mechanism exists, but two or more proposals are at about the same level of maturity, deployment and specification, and the group cannot choose.

The RFC points out why this is hard: each proposal may suit slightly different use cases, so the best choice depends on guesses about future use, and proposals may place costs on different groups. This memo is an Experimental document. It proposes mechanisms for such cases and says they must not take precedence over the IETF's normal way of working.

To measure the experiment, the Last Call sent to the IETF community should say that an alternative mechanism was used and which proposal was chosen.
sections.eli5: Two ideas are equally good, everyone agrees one must win, and nobody will budge. This memo is a toolbox for getting unstuck without breaking the normal way of deciding.

sections.title: Rough Consensus as the Baseline
sections.content:
The RFC quotes a conflict-research source: consensus gives a decision everyone can support, but it can be very slow, has a relatively high chance of failure, and tends to favor people who oppose change, since they only need to refuse every compromise.

"Rough consensus" limits this by making sure individuals or small factions cannot easily block a decision that has general support. "Running code" helps by requiring that objections be technically grounded. Participants are still expected to use their best engineering judgment and to balance their own interests against those of the Internet as a whole.

The RFC does not propose changing these usual mechanisms. It only addresses the case where a group has consensus that a decision is needed but cannot make it by the usual rules.
sections.eli5: Normally a group just needs most people to agree, so one grumpy person cannot stop everything. These new tools are only for when that still does not work.

sections.title: Conditions for Using an Alternative
sections.content:
A working group should consider an alternative only when a choice clearly must be made and continued discussion, refinement and implementation experience cannot make it. The RFC lists four conditions.

  • A clear decision. It is stated in the charter, requirements or other group documents, and the Chair(s) confirm general agreement on it, including a consensus call on whether multiple proposals can advance or only a single one.
  • Proposals in draft form. Each must be an Internet-Draft specified well enough that the Chair(s) believe it could be published. If one option is "do nothing", an explicit draft for it must exist, though it may be written when the process is invoked.
  • Discussion without resolution. The Chair(s) make an explicit call for consensus summarizing the issues. If new technical points appear, discussion continues. When in doubt, the Chair(s) should let discussion go on.
  • An explicit working group Last Call on using an alternative, with a stated comment period. It needs the rough consensus of the group, as judged by the Chair(s).

No working group is ever required to use an alternative process. If the group agrees one is needed but cannot agree which, an external review team is formed.
sections.eli5: Before drawing straws, the group has to be sure the choice is clear, the options are written down, they really talked it out, and most people agree to try a tie-breaker.

sections.title: The Four Alternate Methods
sections.content:
The RFC calls these a straw proposal and describes them as deliberately heavyweight, to show the gravity of invoking them and to keep the wider community informed. Each starts with a public announcement on the IETF-announce mailing list. It summarizes the issue and lists the Internet-Drafts. Earlier alternative procedures existed, and RFC 3127 describes one used to choose between two candidate AAA protocols.

Method one, external review team. Five members meet the NomCom voting-member eligibility rules from RFC 3777. People who posted to the working group list in the previous twelve months, the IESG, the IAB and members of an active NomCom are excluded. If more than five volunteer, five are chosen by the process in RFC 3797. The team has one month, extendable by two weeks by any member, and deliberates on an archived mailing list. Each member writes a decision statement of at most one page that ranks the proposals. Statements are tallied by instant-runoff (preference) voting.

Method two, mixed review team. One designated representative per proposal, typically the principal author, plus six external members. Five are chosen as in method one and the sixth is designated by the IESG as chair, who may also vote. Deliberation and tallying work as in method one.

Method three, qualified short-straw selection. One working group participant decides alone. Volunteers must have contributed in the twelve months before the Last Call, for example by a public list statement, by authoring a draft under consideration, or by a minuted comment at a public meeting. The Chair(s) may not volunteer. Names go to the Chair and the IETF Executive Director within three weeks, and one is picked using RFC 3797. That person names the chosen draft by email.

Method four, random assignment. For the rare decision with no technical content at all, the group may ask IANA to pick randomly from clearly delineated values, guided by RFC 3797. The RFC cites a DNS prefix needed by the IDN working group as an example. In extraordinary circumstances, with IESG approval, IANA may pick among a pool of Internet-Drafts this way.
sections.eli5: There are four tie-breakers: ask five neutral outsiders to rank the choices, ask outsiders plus one fan of each choice, let one qualified volunteer chosen by lot decide, or simply draw at random when the choice does not matter technically.

sections.title: Appeals, Risks and IANA
sections.content:
Decisions made this way can be appealed under the same rules as any other working group decision. The one twist is that the group's consensus to use the alternative method stands in for its consensus on the technical question.

The Security Considerations section is about process risk. Moving to these mechanisms shifts the basis of decision making in the IETF, and forcing an evaluation under these rules may let individuals game the system. The RFC admits that groups stuck on a technical matter may also stick on the procedural one, and that people may fear an end-run around rough consensus. It concludes that the methods are about recognizing the need for compromise in a new way.

The IANA Considerations note only that the short-straw method may require IANA to make random selections among a known set of alternates.
sections.eli5: If someone thinks the result was unfair, they can complain just like for any other group decision. The memo also warns that a tricky person might try to cheat the system.

cells: Ranked one-page statements, tallied by instant-runoff voting
One representative per proposal plus six external members
Ranked statements, tallied by instant-runoff voting
Chosen using RFC 3797, names the selected draft
Random pick from clearly delineated values
